title: Draw Things on a 24 GB Mac: Fast When It Works, Blind Until It Does
dek: Hands-on test on a MacBook Pro with M3 Pro. The first prompt returned a gray square. The second model worked.

seo.title: Draw Things Test on a 24 GB Mac: Fast Once a Model Fits
seo.description: Hands-on test of Draw Things on a 24 GB MacBook Pro (M3 Pro): good images once a suitable model ran, but no hardware hints in the model list.

faq: Does Draw Things run on a 24 GB Mac?

Yes, once a suitable model was installed. On a MacBook Pro with an M3 Pro and 24 GB, ERNIE Image Turbo 1.0 (8-bit S, about 11.4 GiB) produced images in under a minute, per the tester. Downloads of about 25 to 57 GB (FLUX, Chrono Edit 14B, LTX 2.3 22B distilled) were larger than his memory; download size is not the same as runtime memory.
Which model should I start with in Draw Things?

The test does not recommend one. The tester's first choice, SeedVR2 7B, is a video restoration model and returned a gray square for a text prompt. ERNIE Image Turbo 1.0 (8-bit S) worked. A third-party assistant named it among the safest image models for 24 GB; that was not verified.
Its pricing page lists a Free Edition that generates images locally. The tester noticed no paywall but could not tell how the free 'Community' account differs from it. Not verified.
Can Draw Things refine an existing image?
The tester did not find a way to say 'keep this picture and change this'. Version History and Edit tools are visible in the app but were not evaluated.
meta: Draw Things by Draw Things, Inc. Store title at test time: 'Offline AI Art'
MacBook Pro, Apple M3 Pro, 24 GB unified memory (the notes say '24 GB VRAM'; Apple Silicon shares one memory pool)
macOS, current release at the test date; exact version not recorded
Mac App Store. Pricing page: drawthings.ai/pricing
4.6 stars from 175 ratings, age 18+, #8 in Photo & Video, 471 MB

Draw Things ranked #4 in clicks over the last 28 days in the tester's Google Search Console data (scope of the ranking not recorded). Japanese-language clicks exceeded English; Korean was third and Chinese fourth.
Not stated in the notes. Derived from them: install Draw Things on a 24 GB Mac, get a model running, generate images, and try one real task (a hero image for PromptQuorum).
ChatGPT (company research, prompt writing), Perplexity (model advice for 24 GB), Grok (no answer obtained)
disclosure: The tester founded PromptQuorum (promptquorum.com), a content site and directory about local AI apps. Draw Things receives clicks on that site. The notes record no contact with the vendor, no payment and no sponsorship.

verdict.general: Capable, and its pricing page lists a free edition. On a 24 GB M3 Pro it produced good-looking images quickly once a suitable model was installed. The first-run experience is the weak point: the model list the tester saw gave no size, task type or hardware fit, and he could not find how to iterate on a result.
verdict.fit: Not continuing for now ('not for me, not for now'). The tester found no clear way to refine an existing image and could not make sense of the controls, and he keeps cloud chat models for iterative work. Features that appear in screenshots but were not evaluated: Version History, Edit tools, Image Interpreter.

scores_note: Scores are proposals derived from the evidence below (1 = poor, 5 = very good). They are the tester's to confirm.
tldr: Works well once the right model is installed: the tester reports under a minute per image on the M3 Pro.
Getting there is the hard part: a model list with no sizes or hardware fit, downloads of 11 to 16 GiB with no time estimate, and no warning when a video-restoration model was used for a text prompt.
The tester will not continue. He could not find a way to revise an image or understand the controls, but did not evaluate several features visible in his screenshots.
quotes: Overall, very unsatisfying process. [...] You're hunting blind.
It's a simple picture generator, which it does very well on my 24-gigabyte MacBook. It went very fast. It's fine, but that's about it.

chapters.title: The store listing
items: The tester downloaded Draw Things from the Mac App Store. The listing read 'Offline AI Art', developer Draw Things, Inc., 4.6 stars from 175 ratings, age 18+, #8 in Photo & Video, 471 MB.
The listing does not say plainly that the app runs locally beyond 'Offline AI Art'. It names optimization for M1, M2 and M3 and does not mention newer chips (as read by the tester).
Technical specifications are listed without explanation, and limitations are not visible.

chapters.title: First launch: three steps and one long list
items: A welcome dialog (step 1 of 3, English) asks for a model source: Cloud Compute (needs an Apple sign-in), download via Draw Things, or import from local storage. It suggests FLUX.1 as 'mighty and popular'.
Step 2 of 3 lists official models by name and family. File size, task type and hardware hints do not appear in the rows. A search field sits above the list.
Nothing explains which models make pictures and which make video, how they differ, or whether they fit in memory. The tester called the list 'endless' and the process 'hunting blind'.
Correction to the tester's notes: the notes say there is no search window; the screenshot shows one. The finding is therefore limited to missing filters by size, task and hardware.

chapters.title: The memory wall
items: The tester looked for a model that fits 24 GB. As read from the download dialogs: a FLUX model of about 32 GB, Chrono Edit 14B of about 25 GB, and LTX 2.3 22B distilled (6-bit) of about 57 GB. The dialogs for these three are not in the notes.
SeedVR2 7B looked small enough at 16,757.66 MiB (about 16.4 GiB) and was downloaded.
The download dialog shows percentage and MiB, and no remaining time. According to the tester, the rest of the app could not be used while the model downloaded.
A download of this size should show a time estimate, as most apps do.
Setup step 3 of 3 asks where generated images should be saved, inside the same window as the model download. The step is marked optional. The tester asked why it sits in setup.

chapters.title: Pricing, releases and documentation
items: The pricing page lists a Free Edition: 'Create prompts and download models from our servers to generate images locally and privately on your own device', with local compute, model downloads, an infinite canvas and local LoRA training.

The tester could not tell how a free account ('Community') differs from the Free Edition. His reading: the Free Edition runs on your Mac and Community adds cloud compute with usage limits. Not verified.
Release history looked active: roughly one release every two months, by the tester's reading. Exact dates were not recorded.

The documentation has pages for Basic UI, Models, LoRA, ControlNet, Textual inversion, Others, CoreML and Scripts. The Basic UI page shows an image placeholder, and its outline carries an '[old version]' line.
The documentation is shallow and assumes you know what a LoRA is.

chapters.title: First generation: a gray square
items: Prompt: 'red ball please. with gold dot in middle'. The app showed an estimated time of 11 minutes and the tester could hear the computer working. The result was a flat gray square.
A 'Negative' prompt field was active. The tester did not add it and did not know why it was there.

A second attempt used a long ChatGPT-written prompt (Neuschwanstein Castle, Keith Haring style, exactly four colors). Time estimates across the attempts were about 11, 10 and 20 minutes. The notes do not state the result of this attempt; the tester then went looking for the cause.
The tester infers that the estimate does not depend on the prompt. Three data points; the estimate may also reflect the model that was selected.

chapters.title: Finding the cause
items: The app describes SeedVR2 7B as a one-step diffusion video restoration model. It had been selected for both picture attempts.
The tester selected a restoration model for a text-to-image prompt.
The app should have flagged that the model does not fit a text prompt. The notes report no warning.

chapters.title: Asking other AIs
items: Grok did not answer. Perplexity did. For a 24 GB MacBook it named ERNIE Image Turbo 1.0 (6-bit S and 8-bit S) as the safest image models and SeedVR2 7B for upscaling and restoration. It rated LTX-2.3 22B distilled (6-bit) as experimental for short, low-resolution video and advised against the [dev] LTX models and the full ERNIE Base model. Its sources were not checked here.
The app should offer this: enter your hardware and get a pre-filtered list.

chapters.title: It works
items: The tester downloaded ERNIE Image Turbo 1.0 (8-bit S): 11,644.41 MiB, about 11.4 GiB, in 3 files.
This is taken to be the model behind the later images. The notes do not name it.
Images took under a minute each. Times were not recorded.

The Neuschwanstein prompt produced a recognizable castle with Haring-style figures and radiating lines (top of this page). Natural stone, forest and sky tones remain, so the 'exactly four colors' instruction was not met.
A generated motorhome looks convincing, but the lettering on its side is nonsense text. The prompt was not recorded.
Picture quality is great. Text inside pictures is weak.

chapters.title: A real job: a hero image for PromptQuorum
items: The tester asked for a hero image presenting PromptQuorum as 'the world's leading directory for local LLM and local AI apps'. The first attempt used a long prompt (length counter 3,670) and produced a dark interface collage with several garbled labels.
After settings were changed the output became multicolored noise. Text Guidance reads 45.5 in the panel.
The high guidance value caused the noise. The cause was not isolated.
Turning the 'iteration' setting down helped, in the tester's words.
With a shorter prompt (counter 51) the headline became readable. Smaller labels stayed garbled.

chapters.title: Iteration and controls
items: The tester could not find a way to say 'keep this picture and change this', as frontier chat models allow. To start a new image he deleted the old prompt by hand.
Version History (with 'Generated image' and 'Cleared canvas' entries), an 'Edit' button, Canvas Tools, Image Interpreter and CLIP Score are visible in the screenshots. None of them was evaluated.

A first-time user would not understand the controls, and the link between controls and models is unclear. The panel does carry explanatory text, and notes that controls are additional files added on top of models.

chapters.title: Decision
items: The tester will not continue to use the app, even though it is free. Reasons: no easy mode, results are hard to adapt, and it is unclear how to apply a house style or guide the system toward one exact picture.
The tester's view that a local model can produce pictures a cloud model would refuse was not tested.
'Not for me, not for now.' He may lack the know-how to manage such a tool.

claims: 'Offline AI Art'; generate images privately on your own device
Models are downloaded from Draw Things' servers through the app. Generation ran on the Mac (the tester could hear it working). Offline operation was not tested.
Optimized for Apple Silicon, especially M1, M2 and M3
Store listing, as read by the tester
Newer chips are not mentioned in the text the tester read. The app ran on an M3 Pro.
FLUX downloads were about 32 GB for a tester with 24 GB of memory. The dialog shows no fit warning.
The notes mention no paywall. The tester's reading is that all functions are in the free app. Not verified.
The first result was a gray square. With a different model the tester reports under a minute per image.

fit.note: Download size is not runtime memory. The app may load weights on demand, and results depend on quantization and resolution (assumption, based on the third-party answer above). The first three sizes are as read aloud by the tester, in GB.

severity_note: Severity is the impact on a first-time user. Proposed, not measured.

fits: Mac users who already know which diffusion model they want and want a free local image generator.
People who want an infinite canvas and local LoRA training (as listed on the pricing page).
not_fits: First-time users who expect the app to guide them to a model that fits their hardware.
Users who want to refine a picture step by step in a chat-like flow, as the tester found it.
audience.retest: Retest when the model list shows size or hardware fit, or after the next major release. The tester says 'maybe later'; a 3 to 6 month interval would cover several releases (assumption).

background_intro: Not hands-on. This comes from ChatGPT research the tester pasted into his notes, and none of it was verified for this test.
background: Draw Things, Inc. is described as founder-led by Liu Liu. The app launched in November 2022 as a free iPhone app running Stable Diffusion locally (as cited by ChatGPT, source given as Ars Technica).

A company database profile calls it bootstrapped, with 1 to 5 employees, based in San Francisco. No publicly disclosed institutional funding was found. ChatGPT itself cautions that private funding can be undisclosed (source given as ToolJunction).
A community GitHub repository is reported at about 578 stars, 2,100+ commits and 71 releases (source given as Swift Package Index).
Engineering articles are cited for a custom Swift inference stack and Metal FlashAttention work (source given as Medium).
